text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point.
- Each token in the group account pays 0.3 points to every member of the group, you included, whoever put it there.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking: This is a public goods game where contributing to the group yields only 0.3 back per token to me versus keeping 1 privately, so defection is the dominant individual strategy even though full cooperation would raise everyone's payoff. Since the dominant strategy favors keeping tokens, I'm weighing how that logic plays out across repeated rounds.

This is a classic public goods game setup: each contributed token returns only 0.3 to me but 1.2 total to the group, so self-interest favors keeping everything while group welfare favors full contribution—the usual free-rider tension.

With 10 rounds ahead, I could start cooperatively to encourage reciprocity, or just defect for safety. I'll settle on a moderate contribution, maybe 10 tokens, as a middle-ground test of cooperation while explaining my reasoning.
